A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MSRL research. All text, tables, equations and figures support comparison. V1 ends with references; v2 includes readable Appendices A–F and their associated figures.

before.justification: V1 reports original ChartMimic and ReachQA evaluations, SFT scaling experiments, reward and training-stage ablations, and qualitative comparisons.

after.justification: V2 retains these benchmark results and adds original generalization tests, evaluator validation, optimizer and dataset comparisons, and qualitative error analyses.

M1.justification: The backbone, GRPO optimization, textual and visual reward components, and textual-then-hybrid training sequence remain unchanged. V2 clarifies that execution reward is separate from textual accuracy, consistent with the reward equation and weights already reported in v1; this does not establish a new method component.

E1.justification: V2 adds evaluation on Seaborn- and Plotly-style chart images, extending testing beyond the retained ChartMimic and ReachQA benchmarks to unseen visual styles. Appendix C also introduces actual SFT and RL experiments using ChartCoder training data.

E2.justification: The headline benchmark comparator sets are unchanged, but v2 substantially expands controlled comparisons: DPO is evaluated against GRPO, and InternViT and DINOv2-L become alternative visual-reward evaluators. Appendix C also compares five scoring models against human judgments, including GPT-4.1 and InternVL3-38B.

E3.justification: V2 introduces budget-dependent training comparisons, a 200-sample human-scoring evaluation, a 100-sample filtering audit, and DPO preference pairs generated by perturbing 2–3 code attributes. Table 5 selects 5.5k second-stage samples instead of v1's stated 11k, although Appendix B retains 11k, leaving the final training setting inconsistent. The original benchmark splits remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds RL saturation curves, computational-cost analysis, evaluator validation, optimizer and training-data ablations, distribution-shift tests, and explicit failure cases. It replaces v1's Figure 4 reward-training traces and removes the single-stage hybrid and textual-then-visual comparisons, changing the evidence used to justify the curriculum.

E5.justification: Appendix C and Figure A newly estimate Pearson correlations between evaluator scores and human judgments, adding statistical agreement analysis absent from v1. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests for benchmark performance.

E6.justification: The headline benchmark scores remain unchanged, but v2 adds substantial results, including MSRL high-level scores of 30.5 and 35.9 on Seaborn and Plotly images, and DPO versus GRPO comparisons. V1's visual-only scores of 77.8/81.9 survive in Appendix Table B; v2 Table 5 separately reports 79.13/84.01 for a 22k-sample configuration, without establishing a like-for-like performance gain.

T1.justification: V1's Equations 2–3 explicitly define the clipped GRPO objective and normalized advantage. V2 removes these formulations and substitutes a short verbal description, while retaining the weighted reward equation. Neither version supplies original theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The central claims about the SFT plateau, the large training corpus, multimodal rewards and benchmark improvements are retained. V2 narrowly softens novelty by dropping the abstract's claim that competitiveness with advanced closed-source models is achieved 'for the first time'.

C2.justification: V2 reframes the two-stage strategy around computational efficiency rather than primarily training stability and best performance. It interprets visual rewards as effective but expensive, discusses evaluator agreement and alternative optimizers, and adds concrete limitations: invented chart details and imperfect subplot layouts in Appendix D.

D1.justification: V2 newly supplies exact generation, filtering and visual-scoring prompts, chart-type counts and exclusions, the pre-2024 source-paper cutoff, and additional computational-cost information. Its reproducibility statement reports supplementary training and reward code. The existing hyperparameter and hardware description is relocated almost unchanged from Section 4.2 to Appendix B.

R1.justification: V2 broadens citations to work including StructChart, ChartEdit, ChartM3, rendering-aware vector-graphics RL and DINOv2, and adds an explicit dataset comparison. The related-work organization and central positioning remain stable. Publication and author-list updates for existing references do not represent new works.

P1.justification: V2 polishes the abstract, introductory motivation and conclusion, clarifies reward terminology, consolidates reward/stage-ablation discussion, and moves implementation details into the appendix. It adds a reproducibility statement and organized appendices, while retaining most of the main method and results exposition.

P2.justification: V2 adds dataset and generalization tables, evaluator scatter plots, prompt panels, and detailed code-image examples. Figure 4 changes from reward-training traces to data-scaling curves, and the reward/stage tables are reorganized into a comparison containing sample budgets and GPU hours. Most other original main figures are retained.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens scrutiny of the central visual-reward design through human agreement checks and alternative evaluator, optimizer and dataset comparisons. Exact prompts, cost analysis, generalization tests and explicit failure cases address important validation and reproducibility gaps in v1. These gains outweigh the removed ablation controls, although the unresolved 5.5k-versus-11k second-stage setting limits reproducibility of the final configuration.
